newsitem.title: USA: Dollar mixed at US noon as mark scores vs crosses.
newsitem.headline: Dollar mixed at US noon as mark scores vs crosses.

text.p: The dollar pulled back from a six-year high at 1.84 marks, but held its sharp gains on the Swiss franc as the mark charged off its session lows against the crosses, dealers said.
Mark/Swiss made a stunning break toward 0.82 from a low just under 0.81 and dollar/Swiss hit a 43-month high at 1.5033.
"It was mostly profit-taking on the mark, especially against the Swiss. People were short the mark against everything," said Francois Akl, chief dealer at Gulf International Bank in New York.
Dealers attributed the Swiss franc's slide to reports that a U.S. investment bank and a U.S. fund were buying mark/Swiss, and suspected Swiss National Bank liquidity additions.
Dollar/Swiss broke through its March 1997 high at 1.4922, triggering stop-loss buying up toward 1.50 dealers said.

"We saw very large selling of Swiss francs on the break of 1.4925. Dollar/Swiss and dollar/yen may be playing a bit of catch-up to the dollar move versus the Europeans," said Steve Flanagan, vice president at Credit Agricole Indosuez.
In addition, traders wondered if Bank of Italy buying had boosted mark/lira by almost three lira from its session low.
The dollar stood at 1.8290/00 marks at midday, down from 1.8350/55 at the open, but up from 1.8255/65 at Wednesday's close. Dollar/Swiss stood at 1.4990/00, up from 1.4850/55.
Dollar/yen was up slightly at 115.83/88 from 115.58/68, but failed to hold morning gains above 116.

Dollar/mark broke 1.83 in overnight trade, then powered past an August 1991 high at 1.8350 as the Bundesbank entered its four-week summer recess with a fixed repo rate for the first two weeks and no statement condemning the dollar's rise.
The dollar shrugged off the Bundesbank's rare move not to decide on the repo rate for the final two weeks of the recess.
"This is not a knee-jerk type reaction," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank. "We're starting to see real-money people exit the mark."
The dollar's failure to get through 1.84 marks highlights the residual fear of Bundesbank intervention to bolster its currency, dealers said.
But without any real prospects of higher interest rates in Germany, where the domestic economy continues to struggle, dealers said intervention might offer only temporary help.
"The question is: would people take that as an opportunity to buy on the dip," said a U.S. commercial bank trader.
"Without interest rates to back them up, they'd be up the creek. It would have to be a massive intervention to get people to back off," she added.
Barring any signs of official distress, the dollar is expected to continue through 1.84 marks in the near future after a modest amount of profit-taking to reinvigorate dollar bulls, dealers said.

"They'll probe 1.84 and see what's there. People are a little afraid the Bundesbank is above there, but if it's not, there's no reason not to keep buying dollars," said Kevin Lawrie, global foreign exchange manager at Mellon Bank.
In other trade, the dollar rose to Canadian $1.3827/32 from C$1.3813/18 at the open. Sterling fell to $1.6730/40 from $1.6760/70.
((--Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664))
